rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses are reported as revealed during the Prophet’s dispute with Quraysh idolaters over qadar, God’s allocation of provision to creation.
rows.anchor: reported to have been revealed in connection with a dispute between the Prophet and the idolaters among the Quraysh concerning God’s “measuring out”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here qadar, or measuring out, concerns how God gives or withholds provision for all creation.
rows.anchor: which refers to the manner in which God gives or withholds provision for all of creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suʿur, translated “mad,” is related to saʿīr, “blaze,” used in the Quran for Hell’s punishment.
rows.anchor: Mad translates suʿur, which is related to saʿīr, or blaze, a word used throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the verse as saying that disbelievers burn in the Fire, astray in this world and blazing in the next.
rows.anchor: Some thus interpret this verse to mean that the disbelievers are “burning ( yasʿur ) in the Fire”

rows.speaker: author

rows.anchor: Dragged upon their faces likely indicates punishment for various iniquities

rows.speaker: the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse straightforwardly affirms that God created all things.
rows.anchor: This verse can be understood as a straightforward affirmation of God’s creation of all things

rows.speaker: author

rows.anchor: In relation to the preceding verses, it can also be understood as a simple statement that God decreed or “measured” a punishment for the disbelievers and cast them into Saqar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s debate with qadar-deniers made this verse a focus of the dispute over Divine determinism and human choice.
rows.anchor: this verse became a focal point for discussing the relation between Divine determinism and human choice

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet makes belief in qadar, good and evil, and acceptance of what befalls or misses one a condition of true faith.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “No servant of God truly believes until he believes in qadar, its good and evil

rows.speaker: Jabariyyah
rows.claim: The Jabariyyah hold that God determines every human act, including belief, disbelief, good, and evil; they cite 76:30 and 81:29.
rows.anchor: The earliest determinists, known as the Jabariyyah (lit. “Compulsionists”), held that all human acts were determined by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes favoring more human choice stress the precision or perfection of creation’s measure.
rows.anchor: those who favored a greater degree of human choice or self-determination preferred to focus upon the manner in which God has created everything with precision

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators and all recitation schools read kull shayʾ in the accusative, the translation’s form, though it is grammatically problematic.
rows.anchor: the reading preferred by most commentators and found in all schools of recitation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading kull shayʾ in the nominative makes the phrase mean that everything God created is according to a measure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative reading can leave open whether God created everything, supporting a free-will reading associated with Qadarites and Muʿtazilites.
rows.anchor: the early Qadarite theological trend and the Muʿtazilite school of theology

rows.speaker: Qadarites
rows.claim: Qadarites hold that humans are free and author their acts without thereby limiting God’s Omnipotence.
rows.anchor: The Qadarites held that human beings are free and are the authors of their own acts

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites
rows.claim: Muʿtazilites hold humans responsible for creating their evil deeds, absolving a just God from creating acts for which He punishes them.
rows.anchor: The Muʿtazilites held that human beings are fully responsible for the creation of their evil deeds

rows.speaker: Ashʿarite school of theology
rows.claim: Ashʿarites reject Qadarite and Muʿtazilite creators outside God and Jabarite fatalism; God creates all acts while humans remain responsible, as 40:62 affirms.
rows.anchor: The Ashʿarite school of theology finds both of these positions abhorrent, because each would posit a creative agent outside of God

rows.speaker: Ashʿarite theologians
rows.claim: Ashʿarites distinguish God’s creation of acts from human acquisition: people choose among God-created options and thereby acquire their acts.
rows.anchor: Ashʿarite theologians thus sought to explain that God is Just and Merciful and does not punish people for things for which they are not responsible

rows.speaker: commentators favoring Muʿtazilite views
rows.claim: Free-will leaning commentators do not use this verse to prove their position; they emphasize Divine Wisdom in the universe’s precise measure.
rows.anchor: Commentators who incline more toward the Muʿtazilite position and favor a greater degree of free will than that allowed for by the Ashʿarite position

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says creation follows wisdom’s determined measure, or a measure written on the Tablet and known by God before existence, including its state and duration.
rows.anchor: al-Zamakhsharī writes, “We have created everything in a determined measure, ordered according to that which wisdom has decreed

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī says nothing is haphazard: each thing has a known measure and purpose, and changing its measure would defeat its function.
rows.anchor: the Shiite theologian al-Ṭabrisī emphasizes that this verse indicates that nothing has been created haphazardly

rows.speaker: Ashʿarites
rows.claim: Ashʿarite commentators see Divine Wisdom and the Preserved Tablet here; humans acquire acts but cannot create or determine them, while vv. 47–48 criticize those claims.
rows.anchor: Many who are more closely aligned with the Ashʿarite position also see this verse as an expression of the Divine Wisdom

rows.speaker: Ashʿarites
rows.claim: Ashʿarites cite a hadith calling the community’s qadar-deniers its Magians.
rows.anchor: they cite several aḥādīth, among them: “Every community has its Magians, and the Magians of my community are those who say that there is no measuring out

rows.speaker: Ashʿarites
rows.claim: Ashʿarites distinguish pretemporal qaḍāʾ, pertaining to God’s uncreated Essence, from temporal qadar, an attribute of Action contingent with what it brings into being.
rows.anchor: In elaborating upon their understanding of Divine determinism, Ashʿarites identify two stages or aspects of the Divine Decree

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects philosophical necessity: qaḍāʾ concerns God’s Knowledge and qadar His Will, so creation occurs by His willing measure rather than necessity.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī argues against the philosophical notion that it is necessary for things to be created in the manner that they are created

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah says certainty in the measure relieves sorrow and planning, leading one to entrust affairs to God and accept every decree; he alludes to 102:5 and 40:44.
rows.anchor: Thus Ibn ʿAjībah writes: “It washes the heart of sorrows and of all that is other

rows.speaker: al-Maybudī
rows.claim: Al-Maybudī says finding God means having everything, while a person deprived of God has nothing despite possessing everything.
rows.anchor: In this same vein, the commentator al-Maybudī writes of this verse

rows.speaker: Sufi thinkers
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī’s and Mullā Ṣadrā’s schools relate choice and Decree to humanity’s capacity to know the Divine Names, including al-Murīd and al-Qadīr; freedom is itself God-created.
rows.anchor: For many Sufi thinkers, such as those of the school of Ibn ʿArabī

rows.speaker: Sufi thinkers
rows.claim: Sufis see human will as God’s Power and Will manifested, and true freedom as a state attained by rising above ego and submitting one’s individual will to God.
rows.anchor: Rather than seeing the question of human free will as a question merely of choices between options on a particular plane of reality

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī’s paradox is that saints most able to perform miracles are least likely to do so because they accept God’s Will.
rows.anchor: This is exemplified in a paradox discussed by Ibn ʿArabī, who says that those saints

rows.speaker: Sufi thinkers
rows.claim: Sufis understand one’s qadar or lot as one’s essence known by God before creation; God transcends free-will and determinism, while human freedom originates in God’s breathing His Spirit into Adam (32:9).
rows.anchor: Moreover, qadar, or one’s “lot,” is seen, in the ultimate sense, as a manifestation of one’s own nature or essence as known by God before one’s creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recalls 28:88, where all things perish except God’s Face.
rows.anchor: Cf. 28:88: All things perish, save His Face

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses turn the sūrah from earthly blessings in vv. 10–25 to the blessings of the Hereafter in the remaining verses.
rows.anchor: These verses mark an important turn in this sūrah, as vv. 10–25 refer to the blessings or boons of this world

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most take “what is upon it” as the earth, its face, or this world generally, meaning all creation will pass away.
rows.anchor: It is taken by most as a reference to the earth, the face of the earth, or this world in general

rows.anchor: Some theologians who see a distinction between God’s Attributes and God’s Essence maintain that this verse indicates that God’s Attributes will also “pass away”

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī objects that this interpretation would require the wording “nothing remains except the Face of thy Lord.”
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī, however, maintains that for this to be the meaning, one would need to say, “And there remains nothing except the Face of thy Lord.”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some explain the choice of “thy Lord” rather than “God” as closer to this sūrah’s theme of blessing and bounty.
rows.anchor: According to some, the Face of thy Lord is used instead of the Face of God, which is used in several other verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Majesty and Bounty can refer respectively to God’s Attributes of Majesty and Beauty, a common theological division of the Divine Names and Attributes.
rows.anchor: The use of Majesty and Bounty can be seen as a reference to God’s Attributes of Majesty and God’s Attributes of Beauty

rows.speaker: many Shiites
rows.claim: Many Shiites call Beauty the positive attributes inherent in God’s Essence and expressing perfection; Majesty negates limiting physical qualities, thereby reaffirming positive attributes.
rows.anchor: For many Shiites the Attributes of Beauty are those positive attributes that are inherent in God’s Essence

rows.anchor: For the difference between the two Gardens described in vv. 62–76 and vv. 48–60, see 55:48c

rows.speaker: author

rows.anchor: This is taken by some to indicate that the ground of these two Gardens is covered with thick vegetation

rows.speaker: author

rows.anchor: Fire is a reminder insofar as it reminds one of the Resurrection or the Fire in Hell

rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “This fire of yours that human beings kindle contains but a seventieth of the heat in Hell”

rows.anchor: is a Madinan sūrah

rows.anchor: some commentators maintain that only the first ten verses are from the Madinan period and the remainder is from the Makkan period

rows.anchor: others maintain that the entire sūrah is Madinan except for v. 9

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah’s dispute with her husband Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit over ẓihār, and is also called al-Ẓihār.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the story of a woman named Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah, whose husband, Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓihār was the pre-Islamic formula “You are to me as my mother’s back,” freeing a husband from duties while barring his wife from leaving or remarrying.
rows.anchor: in which a man could renounce his wife by saying, “You are to me as my mother’s back.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khawlah complained to the Prophet and God about the injustice; her plea was heard and a way was provided for reconciliation.
rows.anchor: Khawlah complained of this injustice to the Prophet and to God. Her plea was heard, and God provided a means whereby she and her husband could reconcile

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mujādilah begins a sequence of ten Madinan sūrahs addressing legal issues facing the newly independent Muslim community in Madinah.
rows.anchor: Al-Mujādilah is the first in a series of ten Madinan sūrahs addressing many of the legal issues

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence follows 57:4, which says God knows what enters and leaves earth and Heaven, is with people wherever they are, and sees their deeds.
rows.anchor: follows upon the statement in 57:4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s Omnipresence is foregrounded by the first four verses’ immediate response to a Muslim woman’s plea.
rows.anchor: God’s Omnipresence is especially indicated in this sūrah, as the first four verses provide an example of God’s responding directly and instantly to the plea of a Muslim woman

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–4 address ẓihār; verses 5–6 introduce opponents of God and His Messenger, the theme of the rest of the sūrah.
rows.anchor: vv. 5–6 introduce the discussion of those who oppose God and His Messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 7–10 treat opponents’ secret conversations and derision of the Prophet, then prescribe proper private discourse.
rows.anchor: Vv. 7–10 discuss the secret converse of those who oppose and deride the Prophet and the proper manner in which to hold private discourse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–13 first enjoin almsgiving before private conversation with the Prophet, then ease that injunction.
rows.anchor: vv. 11–13, which initially enjoin Muslims to offer alms before conversing with the Prophet and then lighten this injunction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long section in verses 14–21 addresses hypocrites and their opposition to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: The longest section, vv. 14–21, addresses the nature of the hypocrites and their opposition to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes with a long verse on God’s rewards for those who believe in God and the Last Day.
rows.anchor: the sūrah concludes with a long verse regarding the rewards that God gives to those who believe in God and the Last Day
